summary:
Paraná is a state of Brazil and stands under Brazil's national framework. Paraná is assessed at the national score: no deviation from the national position has been identified that is material enough to score separately (within ±0.02). A visitor to Curitiba or anywhere else in the state therefore faces the same law as a visitor to any other part of the country.

Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since May 2013, under National Council of Justice Resolution 175/2013, which binds all civil registries after a 14-1 vote, and adoption rights have followed since 2015. An expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a trans visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in family matters.

The Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, and in 2023 the Superior Court of Justice allowed nonbinary people to amend their civil records. The age of consent is equal regardless of sexual orientation, and lesbian, gay and bisexual people serve openly in the armed forces.

On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Tribunal ruled that discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is a crime equivalent to racism under Lei 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines, and transphobia is now punished on the same footing as racism. No specific federal anti-discrimination statute exists behind that ruling, and repeal efforts have been mounted in Congress, so the protection rests on constitutional and criminal provisions rather than a dedicated statute. Intersex people have no specific protections in Brazilian law.

The protective text of the law does not describe what people routinely encounter. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions. A May 2024 investigation documented 'boa noite, Cinderela' drink-spiking robberies in which LGBTQIA+ people are targeted in São Paulo nightlife, in a city preparing for a Pride event that draws thousands of tourists. In the October 2024 municipal elections, close to 1,000 transgender candidates stood across every state of the country and received death threats and intimidation, while the number of trans officeholders tripled compared with the previous cycle.

Detention carries a specific and contested regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. A person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing. On arrest the place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a judge in a reasoned decision after the person has been consulted about their preference; the judge must set out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell. The declared preference is recorded, a later change of placement is possible, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

Practice does not reliably follow that framework. A peer-reviewed census of travestis and transgender women held in Rio de Janeiro state prisons, carried out between April and June 2021, interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine in the metropolitan region. It documents that in that system travestis and trans women are housed in units operated as masculine, with some held in so-called neutral or security units, and treats placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. The same study notes a 2015 Rio de Janeiro state law granting parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units, covering hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics, and national norms from 2014 and 2020 that permit people to be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine. Rio de Janeiro is one province's evidence of how the national detention rules are applied, not a finding about Paraná's own prison system.
tangentialFactors:
Courts have applied the 2019 provisions to commercial conduct. The 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing, affirming the compensation ordered at first instance in Barra Bonita. Refusal of service on gender-identity grounds has therefore produced a civil damages order in at least one documented case.

An analysis of case law from 2022 records lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women, bringing trans people within the country's violence-prevention statutes. The direction of that litigation is protective, but the analysis describes pressure on the court rather than a settled national holding.

The statutory base of the protection is contested in the legislature. Outright International reports that Congress has repeal efforts under way, and that no specific federal anti-discrimination statute exists to anchor the 2019 ruling. Intersex people remain outside the specific protections that cover sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds.

Violence indicators are national rather than provincial. The drink-spiking robberies documented in May 2024 occurred in São Paulo nightlife, and the death threats and intimidation directed at close to 1,000 transgender candidates in the October 2024 municipal elections were recorded across every state of the country. Neither source isolates a rate for Paraná.

outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory reports Paraná-specific enforcement of the June 2019 ruling, Paraná-specific prosecutions for SOGI discrimination, or outcomes for complaints filed in the state. Whether the protection is applied in practice in Paraná is unresolved on the available material.

No Paraná data is sourced on where trans, travesti and intersex detainees are actually placed under Resolution 348/366, or on whether the self-declaration procedure is followed at custody hearings in the state. The census documenting placement in units operated as masculine was conducted in Rio de Janeiro state prisons between April and June 2021 and cannot be read across to Paraná without further evidence.

No Paraná-specific figures are sourced for violence against trans people, for drink-spiking or nightlife robberies of the kind documented in São Paulo in May 2024, or for threats against trans candidates in the October 2024 municipal elections in this state.

The status of the repeal efforts in Congress reported by Outright International is not resolved in the inventory: no date, stage or outcome of any such bill is sourced. Whether the Superior Court of Justice has since issued a national holding extending the Maria da Penha Law and Feminicide Law remedies to trans women, as the 2022 case-law analysis describes lower courts urging, is likewise not sourced here.

Intersex-specific protections are recorded as absent, but no source addresses intersex medical or documentation practice in Paraná.
